## Purpose

We asked whether EpiEstim's intervals for the instantaneous reproduction number
were too wide or too narrow, and whether this depended on the number of observed
cases and the estimation window. A simulated epidemic gives us a reference
$R_t$ for each day. At a given population size and window setting, each
independent series of case counts contributes one estimate to the comparison.

## 1. Simulation setup

We solved a deterministic SIR model on the proportion scale for days 0 to 100,
with $R_0=2$, a mean infectious period of five days and an initial infectious
proportion of $10^{-4}$. If $S_t$ is the susceptible proportion, the reference
reproduction number is $R_t=R_0 S_t$. Multiplying the daily incidence rate
$\beta S_t I_t$ by population size gives the expected count used below.

```{r}

sir_model = function(t, R0, g) {
  
  init <- c(S=1-1e-4, I=1e-4, R=0)
  parameters <- c(beta=R0 * g, gamma=g)
  time <- seq(0,t,length.out = t+1)
  
  eqn <- function(time,state,parameters){
    with(as.list(c(state,parameters)),{
      dS <- -beta*S*I
      dI <- beta*S*I-gamma*I
      dR <- gamma*I
      return(list(c(dS,dI,dR)))})
  }
  out = deSolve::ode(y=init,times=time,eqn,parms=parameters)
  out = as.data.frame(out)
  out %>% mutate(
    R_t = R0 * S,
    incid = parameters["beta"]*S*I
  )
  
}

tmp = sir_model(100, 2, 1/5)

ggplot(tmp, aes(x=time))+
  geom_line(aes(y=S,colour = "susceptible"))+
  geom_line(aes(y=I,colour = "infected"))+
  geom_line(aes(y=incid,colour = "new cases"))+
  geom_line(aes(y=R,colour = "recovered"))

ggplot(tmp, aes(x=time))+
  geom_line(
    aes(y=R_t,colour = "R_t")
    
  )

```

### Population sizes and observed counts

We used 100 rounded, log-spaced population sizes from 316 to 100,000.
At each size we kept the epidemic curve fixed and generated 100 independent
series of observed daily counts. On each day the number observed was a binomial
draw from the rounded model count with ascertainment probability 0.5. There
was no observation delay.

```{r}
scenarios = tidyr::crossing(
  N = round(10 ^ seq(2.5,5,length.out=100)),
  pObs = 0.5, #c(0.2, 0.8),
  run = 1:100
) %>% 
  dplyr::cross_join(tmp) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    cases = round(incid*N),
    obs = rbinom(dplyr::n(), cases, pObs)
  ) %>%
  dplyr::group_by(run,N,pObs) %>%
  dplyr::glimpse()

# ggplot(scenarios, aes(x=time, group=run))+
#   facet_grid(as.factor(N) ~ as.factor(pObs), scales = "free")+
#   geom_step(aes(y=obs))
  
```

## 2. Estimating $R_t$ with EpiEstim

For each series we chose one endpoint uniformly from incidence-vector indices
40 to 75. At that endpoint we fitted EpiEstim using five windows, with
`t_end - t_start` equal to 2, 4, 7, 10 or 14. These are the labels used in
the figures. EpiEstim includes both endpoints, so the corresponding windows
contain 3, 5, 8, 11 or 15 daily counts. We used a parametric serial interval
with mean and standard deviation both five days, and a prior for $R_t$ with
mean 2 and standard deviation 5.

The first entry of the incidence vector is simulation day 0. A window ending
at index 40 therefore includes counts through day 39. The join below compares
it with the reference $R_t$ on day 40. This one-day difference matters when
interpreting bias because $R_t$ falls over the course of this epidemic.

```{r}

results = scenarios %>% dplyr::group_modify(function(d,g,...) {
  
  # Fit all five windows at one endpoint in this replicate.

  endpoint = sample(50-14,1) + 14 +25
  starts = endpoint-c(2,4,7,10,14)
  ends = rep(endpoint,length(starts))
  
  ee = suppressWarnings(EpiEstim::estimate_R(
    incid = data.frame(I = d$obs),
    method = "parametric_si",
    config = EpiEstim::make_config(
      method = "parametric_si",
      mean_si = 5, std_si = 5,
      t_start = starts, t_end = ends,
      mean_prior = 2, std_prior = 5
    )
  ))
  
  tmp = d %>% 
    # filter(obs>0) %>% 
    inner_join(
      ee$R %>% 
        mutate(window = t_end-t_start) %>%
        select(time = t_end, window=window, mean=`Mean(R)`, sd = `Std(R)`), 
      by = "time"
    )
  
  return(tmp)
  
})
```


## 3. Scoring

We used each posterior mean and standard deviation to specify a gamma
distribution for $R_t$. For each population size and window setting we scored
the 100 estimates together, fitting one median location shift on the log
scale. Each point therefore summarises 100 independent series. Comparisons
across windows are paired because the five fits use the same series and endpoint.

The horizontal axis is the largest daily count observed across all 100 series
at that population size. All five window settings share that value. We left
`calibration` unspecified because the spread-to-error ratio is unknown. The
threshold $R_t=1$ is used by the package for its separate classification
summary.

```{r}

tmp = scenarios %>% dplyr::group_by(N,pObs) %>% dplyr::summarise(max_obs = max(obs))

scores = results %>%
  dplyr::transmute(
    window,
    true_value= R_t, location = mean, scale = sd, link="log", dist="gamma2",
    calibration=NA_real_
  ) %>%
  dplyr::group_by(N, pObs, dist, link, calibration, window) %>%
  prediction_scores(threshold = 1) %>% 
  dplyr::inner_join(tmp, by=c("N","pObs"))


plotdata = scores %>% ungroup() %>% mutate(
  H0_B_pit = b_pit_significance(B_pit = B_pit, n_predictions = n_predictions) %>% pull(p_value) > 0.05,
  H0_U_pit = u_pit_significance(U_pit = U_pit, n_predictions = n_predictions) %>% pull(p_value) > 0.05,
  H0_D_pit = d_pit_significance(D_pit = D_pit, n_predictions = n_predictions) %>% pull(p_value) > 0.05,
  `P(obs)`=as.factor(pObs),
  window = as.factor(window)
  # timing = cut(time, c(-Inf,30,60,Inf), labels=c("growth","peak","resolution"))
)

signif = tibble(
  n_predictions = 100,
  B_crit = b_pit_significance(B_pit = NA, n_predictions = n_predictions),
  U_crit = u_pit_significance(U_pit = NA, n_predictions = n_predictions),
  D_crit = d_pit_significance(D_pit = NA, n_predictions = n_predictions)
)
```

## 4. Results

```{r}

p5a = ggplot(plotdata, aes(x=max_obs,y=bias, colour=window))+

  xlab("peak observed case count")+
  ylab("baseline pit-w")+
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype="solid")+
  geom_hline(yintercept = signif$B_crit$critical_0.05, linetype="dashed")
  #+
  #scale_color_manual(values=list("TRUE"="blue","FALSE"="red"), guide=NULL)

p5c = ggplot(plotdata, aes(x=max_obs, colour = window, y=D_pit))+
  geom_point()+
  geom_smooth(se=TRUE)+
  scale_x_log10()+

  ylab("directed pit-w")+

  geom_hline(yintercept = signif$D_crit$critical_0.05, linetype="dashed")+
  geom_hline(yintercept = -signif$D_crit$critical_0.05, linetype="dashed")

  #+
  #scale_color_manual(values=list("TRUE"="blue","FALSE"="red"), guide=NULL)
# 
p5d = ggplot(plotdata, aes(x=max_obs, colour = window,y=U_pit))+
  geom_point()+
  geom_smooth(se=TRUE)+
  scale_x_log10()+
  xlab("peak observed case count")+
  ylab("undirected pit-w")+
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype="solid")+
  geom_hline(yintercept = signif$U_crit$critical_0.05, linetype="dashed")

p5 = p5a+p5b+p5c+p5d+patchwork::plot_layout(guides="collect",axes="collect")+
  patchwork::plot_annotation(tag_level="A")

.gg_save_as(
  p5,
  file.path(fig_dir, "fig4-epiestim-by-epi-size"),
  size = std_size$two_third,
  formats = c("pdf", "eps")
)

```

### Interpretation

Panel A shows mean bias on the $R_t$ scale, calculated as the predictive
median minus the reference and averaged over the 100 series. EpiEstim tended
to overestimate $R_t$, particularly for the longer windows. A longer window
includes earlier days when $R_t$ was higher. The day used for the reference
also contributes to this comparison.

The baseline distance in panel B measures the departure from uniformity before
any adjustment. After adjusting for location, the directed score in panel C
tends to be negative at low counts and positive at high counts. The change
from conservative to overconfident estimates occurred at different case counts
for different windows. Panel D shows the magnitude of the remaining departure.
Its minimum also varies with the window setting.

The dashed lines use $n=100$. For the baseline distance the reference is the
large-sample distribution for independent uniform PIT values. For the two
adjusted scores the reference assumes a common-scale Gaussian model on the
link scale. The fitted gamma distributions have varying scales, so those two
lines provide benchmarks for reading the figure.

```{r}


p6a = ggplot(plotdata, aes(x=max_obs, colour = window,y=mean_crps))+
  geom_point()+
  geom_smooth(se=TRUE)+
  scale_x_log10()+
  xlab("peak observed case count")+
  ylab("mean CRPS")

p6b = ggplot(plotdata, aes(x=max_obs, colour = window,y=mean_coverage.0.5))+
  geom_point()+
  geom_smooth(se=TRUE)+
  scale_x_log10()+
  xlab("peak observed case count")+
  ylab("unadj IQR coverage")+
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, linetype="solid")

p6c = ggplot(plotdata, aes(x=max_obs, colour = window,y=mean_coverage.0.5_adj))+
  geom_point()+
  geom_smooth(se=TRUE)+
  scale_x_log10()+
  xlab("peak observed case count")+
  ylab("adj IQR coverage")+
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, linetype="solid")

# p6d = ggplot(plotdata, aes(x=max_obs, colour = window,y=P_misclass))+
#   geom_point()+
#   geom_smooth(se=TRUE)+
#   scale_x_log10()+
#   xlab("peak observed case count")+
#   ylab("P(misclassification)")


p6 = p6a+p6b+p6c+patchwork::plot_layout(guides="collect",axes="collect")+
  patchwork::plot_annotation(tag_level="A")

p6

```

Panel A gives mean CRPS in units of $R_t$. It measures overall predictive
performance, so it can improve as the estimates become more precise even when
their intervals cover too few reference values. Panels B and C show the
fraction of reference values inside the posterior interquartile range before
and after fitting the common location shift. The horizontal line marks the nominal 50% coverage.

For example, at the largest population the shortest window covered the
reference on `r with(plotdata, round(100 * mean_coverage.0.5[N == max(N) & window == "2"]))`%
of occasions. After the common location adjustment, coverage was
`r with(plotdata, round(100 * mean_coverage.0.5_adj[N == max(N) & window == "2"]))`%.
For the longest window the corresponding figures were
`r with(plotdata, round(100 * mean_coverage.0.5[N == max(N) & window == "14"]))`% and
`r with(plotdata, round(100 * mean_coverage.0.5_adj[N == max(N) & window == "14"]))`%.
The location shift accounts for more of the coverage deficit in the shorter window.

### Scope of the comparison

The prior, ascertainment probability and epidemic trajectory were held fixed.
These simulations show how the scores vary with the available counts and
window setting along that trajectory. They do not establish which window to
use in a new outbreak or isolate how much of the discrepancy comes from the
prior, the window lag or the renewal model.
